analysis.investment_thesis: Arvind is a near-stagnant textile conglomerate with 0.4% revenue CAGR over nine years, ROE of only 9.32%, and a promoter holding of just 39.53% — failing three of my most non-negotiable criteria simultaneously. At 24x earnings for this quality of business, the market is pricing in a future this company has not yet earned.
key_strengths: Debt steadily reduced from INR 2,640 Cr (2020) to INR 1,537 Cr (2025) — showing some financial discipline
Operating cash flow positive all 5 years (INR 595–763 Cr range) — real cash-generating business
Gross margin of 49.1% suggests some brand/product differentiation in textiles
key_risks: Promoter holding at only 39.53% — well below my 55% floor; low skin in the game is a trust concern
Capex surging to INR 535 Cr in FY25 with CWIP jumping to INR 331 Cr — aggressive expansion that has already crushed FCF from INR 687 Cr (2021) to INR 280 Cr (2025)
Commodity textile sector with structural competition from Bangladesh and Vietnam; diversification into real estate, telecom, e-commerce signals lack of core focus
red_flags: Revenue essentially flat for 9 years: INR 8,011 Cr (2016) to INR 8,329 Cr (2025) — 0.4% CAGR
ROE of 9.32% — barely half my 15% minimum threshold
Net loss in FY2021 (-INR 27 Cr) confirms earnings are cyclically vulnerable, not resilient
P/E of 24.1x is expensive for a business with near-zero growth and sub-10% ROE
Debt/Equity of 0.39 exceeds my hard limit of 0.3; cash of only INR 53 Cr vs total debt of INR 1,562 Cr is thin cover
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Arvind fails my fundamental filter on almost every dimension. A 9-year revenue CAGR of 0.4% is not a growth business — it is a business treading water. EBITDA has actually declined at -3.1% CAGR over the same period, meaning profitability has compressed even as revenue held flat. ROE of 9.32% tells me capital is being employed poorly; my benchmark is a minimum 15%, targeting 18-22% for core holdings. I would not pay 24x earnings for a business that earns less than 10% on equity and has shown a net loss as recently as FY2021. The Lalbhai family's promoter holding of 39.53% is deeply concerning — a founder-quality business should have promoters with heavy ownership and aligned long-term interest. When promoters hold less than 40%, the margin of trust is thin.

The FY2025 capital expenditure of INR 535 Cr — nearly double the prior year and three times FY2022 levels — with CWIP jumping to INR 331 Cr is a major red flag right now. This has already compressed FCF from a healthy INR 496 Cr (FY2023) to just INR 280 Cr (FY2025). If this capex does not generate strong returns, the company will have borrowed its way into a lower-quality balance sheet. Debt/Equity at 0.39 already breaches my hard limit of 0.3. The conglomerate structure — textiles, advanced materials, real estate, telecom, e-commerce, agriculture — is precisely the kind of unfocused sprawl I avoid. Arvind is not a bad company; it is a mediocre company priced as if it were a good one. I would need to see the price halve and the business focus sharpen materially before I would revisit.
